The victims of these appalling crimes and their families deserve the truth. I'll begin by paying tribute to my colleague Paul Marr for the powerful and courageous way in which he opened this debate. Every Member here present, and those that could not be, should imagine being the victim or the parent fighting for answers, only to be ignored or failed by the authorities that are meant to protect them.

Grooming gangs represent some of the most sickening organised criminality our country has witnessed. Unless we establish the full scale of what has happened and confront the failures that allowed it to happen, we cannot protect children going forward. Last year, the Welsh Government claimed there were no current widespread issues with grooming gangs in Wales. Let's have a look at the past 10 weeks alone.

On 10 July, Azad Ahmed and Wasee Shikel were imprisoned in Cardiff. On 15 July, eight men were charged across south Wales as part of Operation Oak. On 3 August, five people in Rhyl were convicted of grooming gang offences. That is why our motion calls on the UK Government to ensure that Wales is investigated at the earliest opportunity as part of the statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs. Victims in Wales deserve the same truth, the same justice and the same accountability as victims elsewhere in the United Kingdom. Those cases demand answers. How can the Welsh Government confidently claim there is no widespread problem when serious gaps remain in the evidence?

Reports elsewhere in Britain have identified cases involving predominantly Pakistani-heritage Muslim men targeting white British girls. For years, legitimate questions about those patterns were avoided by the authorities, who seemed more concerned about causing offence than protecting children. We cannot allow political correctness or institutional cowardice to stand in the way of safeguarding.

If similar patterns exist in Wales, they must be exposed. Transparent data on offender ethnicity is essential to understanding the threat and preventing further abuse. The Welsh Government must also scrutinise every relevant policy, including its nation of sanctuary approach, to ensure proper safeguards prevent dangerous individuals from entering or remaining in our communities.

An abuser is an abuser. Correct. Yes. 

Compassion cannot mean naivety. Anyone who comes to this country must respect our laws, our culture, and the rights of women and girls. We need to know whether social services, police forces and local authorities failed in their duty of care, whether warning signs were ignored, and most importantly, what has changed. Victims have waited far too long. They deserve truth, justice and accountability, and this Senedd must not rest until they receive them.

That's the speech over, but I've got a few minutes, so I've got free reign, Llywydd, if you don't mind. Some of the voices here today have been brilliant, and they've got to the heart of the problem. We have an issue going on across our land, and we need to grasp that mantle and do whatever we need to do to ensure our future generations and our young children now are safe and kept safe. There have been some brilliant points made from across the parties. Beca, I agree with many of the points that you made. This should not be a political football; it's a shame you never got the memo.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. First, I'd like to thank the Minister for the statement. Newport and Islwyn have seen a worrying number of pub and hospitality closures in the past few years. These businesses are at the heart of our communities, yet they continue to face mounting pressure from rising costs. Their closure results in lost jobs, reduced economic activity, lower footfall in our town centres and the loss of valuable community spaces. It also reduces the opportunity for young people to gain vital first-job experience and develop the skills needed to enter the wider workforce.

Whilst the Welsh Government's 30 per cent reduction in business rates is welcome, many hospitality businesses continue to face significant financial pressures. As David Chapman, and I'll quote, from UKHospitality Cymru has observed, running a hospitality business in this current climate is like

'plate spinning when you're riding an exercise bike'.

It's a good start, but we must go further. Given the continued loss of jobs in community pubs across Newport and Islwyn, does the Cabinet Minister believe that a 30 per cent reduction in business rates goes far enough? And what further action will the Welsh Government take to support the sector to prevent further closures? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
contributions.text_english: Minister, the most recent available data published by the Office for National Statistics demonstrates that the net fiscal deficit for Wales in 2024-25 was between £22 billion and £23 billion, the second largest fiscal deficit per person of any country or region in the United Kingdom. Only Northern Ireland had a larger per capita fiscal deficit. Expenditure per capita in Wales in 2024-25 was higher than the UK average, while revenue per capita was below the UK average. Has the Welsh Government made any assessment as to the net public sector fiscal balance in Wales for the 2025-26 fiscal year, and does the Minister accept that Wales is a net fiscal beneficiary of the United Kingdom's fiscal transfers?

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, the Bassaleg residents of Forge Mews have been abandoned from the life we all know for close to five years. The old Bassaleg bridge was deemed to be unfit to be unfit for use, leaving the residents with no direct access to their properties other than on foot. Newport City Council have attempted to resolve the matter, but due to funding needs denied by the former Welsh Labour Government in the last Senedd, they are still locked out of normal life, with a resolution still to be found. Imagine, Minister, five years of having to walk home instead of arriving on your own doorstep, five years of having to factor in extra travel time for work or school runs, five years of having to rely on emergency access for fire, ambulance and police support delaying response times, and five years of seeing your house price fall in value, locking you into negative equity. Those residents don't have to imagine; it's their lived reality. To add insult to injury, the council has not even offered them a reduction in their council tax across the last five years, despite a clear lack of services for them. Will the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning agree to meet with me and the resident body to find a lasting solution to their plight?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english:
Could I thank the Cabinet Minister today for bringing forward this statement on the new development agency for Wales? Cabinet Minister, residents in Newport and Islwyn of course want to see increased productivity, an increase in economic growth and, in particular, Welsh businesses supported. Because, regretfully, Newport and Islwyn see some of the worst economic outcomes in the whole of Wales, and has already seen major industry leave over the past years, in particular steel, and the reduction of exports from ports.

For this agency to be successful, businesses need financial certainty, and they need to be able to plan for the years to come. Cabinet Minister, what assurances can you give to multi-year funding cycles, to ensure businesses get the certainty they need? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
contributions.text_english:
I must state an interest as a former soldier and a Ministry of Defence contractor. It is clear, with the current advancement in artificial intelligence, the internet of things, data centres, 5G technology, and the current demand for semiconductors, we will only see an upwards trajectory. Add in the various needs of the weapons industry in the British military, and we ourselves have a vital asset within Casnewydd Islwyn, and I for one am proud they've chosen Newport as their home. Their pathway is to employ 500, rising to 900, in highly skilled, well-paid jobs and, as my colleague has already stated, massively above the common average for the area itself. The chief technology officer has already stated, and I quote him directly, that they will draw upon the skilled workforce of Newport.

Given that the UK Government deems this worthy of circa £250 million plus planned investment over the coming years, and much of this coming from the parent company themselves, what are the Minister's plans to ensure that the vital industry will have the support of the Government going forward, and to assist them by lowering energy costs?

contributions.text_english: First Minister, it's now been 440 days since the Supreme Court ruled that the legal definition of a woman under the Equality Act 2010 referred to biological sex and not gender identity. Does the First Minister not agree that 440 days is a very long time in which to wait for the essential protections outlined in the ruling, which are still being denied to 51 per cent of the population and ignored across multiple sectors, including governmental, education, health and the commercial sector? Numerous cases across the UK are being brought forward and won, correctly, based on this ruling. The Equality and Human Rights Commission recently provided an updated code of practice for services, public functions and associations. This code has specific provisions for the creation of single-sex spaces. Do we wait and dither, allowing such cases to be brought here in Wales, or will the Welsh Government issue a definitive timeline on how and when they intend to update the policies and guidance in Wales in light of these developments? And does the First Minister respect the ruling of the Supreme Court?
